title: Symmetry Mesh - Marketplace & On‑Prem Connector Deep Dive
summary: Focused technical sync on marketplace listing requirements and on-prem connector design for a hybrid service-mesh customer. Discussed packaging options (Helm/operator vs OCI bundle), KMS/HSM integration, signed artifacts, air-gapped UAT approach, and performance expectations for Redwood Private. Agreed next steps: share packaging checklist, run a 1-week connectivity POC, and provide an initial latency/cost projection for their mesh sidecar traffic pattern.
topics: performance bench for small-seq chat workloads

transcript:
[00:00] Avery: Hey everyone thanks for joining, we want to make this pretty technical but also pragmatic, we'll try to map what Symmetry needs for a marketplace listing plus how the private connector would look in your onprem clusters.
[00:12] Lara: Sounds good. thanks. um, today Evan and Priya are here, Tom too. we want to avoid surprises, especially around air-gapped installs and image signing.
[00:23] Marcus: Quick intro, I'm Marcus from Redwood infra team, I run onprem deployments and benching for dedicated/private. we'll cover operator vs Helm, OCI bundle options, and KMS flow.
[00:34] Evan: One quick context note: our clusters are service-mesh heavy, we use sidecar proxies and a control plane that mutates pods; any network egress needs to be reviewed by security, so we may need outbound firewall exceptions or an egress proxy.
[00:50] Priya: and on security: we require signed images and a KMS that either uses our HSM or a cloud HSM via a private peering; we also keep audit logs for 2 years.
[01:05] Avery: Great—so on the marketplace side there are typically two packaging paths: a lightweight Helm chart referencing Redwood's operator, or a fully self-contained operator bundle/OCI image which is easier for air-gapped installs. Helm is simplest for cloud-connected installs, operator/OCI is better for your air-gapped.
[01:25] Tom: Can you explain the tradeoff? we prefer less ops, but air-gapped is a hard req for some of our customers.
[01:33] Marcus: Sure — Helm chart approach means the cluster pulls Redwood container images from the public registry. That requires either proxying to an internal registry mirror or short-lived egress exceptions. With OCI bundle we provide signed images and a tarball you can import to your private registry—so no outbound required. The onboarding script handles RBAC and CRDs.
[01:52] Lara: The OCI bundle sounds promising. How do you handle image signing and verification?
[01:58] Avery: We support Cosign signatures today; the operator verifies signatures at install-time by default. For HSM-backed verification we can integrate with your KMS via PKCS#11 or a cloud HSM tunnel, Marcus can cover specifics.
[02:15] Marcus: Right. For HSM we have two modes: 1) Redwood-managed verification where we keep signatures and you pull artifacts from our signed registry, or 2) customer-managed keys where signing happens inside your CI after you import our bundles. For private deployments we recommend customer-managed key material for maximum compliance. There's a small ops step but it gives you full chain of custody.
[02:38] Priya: Okay—that second mode is preferable. Does your operator validate signatures on every restart, or only at install?
[02:45] Marcus: Default is install-time validation plus weekly background checks. We can enable strict runtime verification on every image load but that adds 2–5 seconds to pod start time depending on your cluster.
[03:01] Evan: About network flow: we have a corporate egress proxy and strict NAT. How does the connector establish control-plane connectivity to Redwood for telemetry and model pulls?
[03:12] Avery: We offer a pull model and a push model. For air-gapped, it's purely pull via your private registry. For hybrid connected clusters, we establish an outbound TLS connection to a Redwood relay endpoint—small outbound only, no inbound. We can also route through your proxy with SNI passthrough.
[03:30] Lara: What about metering and billing? marketplace expects metering hooks for usage-based billing, we need to reconcile with our billing and broker.
[03:39] Marcus: For marketplace listing we expose usage via an agent that emits metrics to a local aggregator. You can configure either a push to the marketplace metering endpoint (if connected) or a daily signed CSV that you upload into the marketplace console. For fully air-gapped, the signed CSV flow is standard.
[03:58] Tom: Is the CSV signed? we need non-repudiation for billing.
[04:02] Avery: Yes—CSV tokenized and signed with our marketplace signing key. For extra control, we can produce invoices with line items per model, token counts, and peak concurrency windows.
[04:14] Priya: On compliance: audit retention and who has access to logs — we need role-based access with SSO and SAML.
[04:22] Avery: Redwood supports SAML SSO for the console and RBAC at token/route level. For Private deployments, audit logs can be forwarded to your SIEM (syslog or HTTPS) and we can set retention policies locally. We'll include architecture docs for that.
[04:38] Evan: Performance question — our main use case is mesh sidecar prefetching small chat contexts, ~80–150 tokens on average, lots of small concurrent flows. We care about tail latency under 120ms. Can Redwood deliver under those constraints on Private?
[04:56] Marcus: Tail latency is sensitive to sequence length and batching. For small sequences and many concurrent requests, the runtime uses continuous batching and KV cache to reduce compute. On a 4-GPU pool with our optimized kernels, we typically hit p50=30–45ms and p95 around 120–160ms depending on quantization. If you need sub-120 p95 we can size for more GPUs or enable latency-optimized routing which disables some batching. We'll run a targeted bench against your traffic profile.
[05:26] Lara: How would quantization affect quality? we have user-facing chat so quality is important.
[05:31] Marcus: There's always a tradeoff. 8-bit quantization is usually acceptable for chat and reduces memory/cost by ~30–40%. We provide per-model quality regressions metrics and can pin a specific model revision. Redwood Optimize can suggest quantization profiles based on your eval prompt set.
[05:50] Tom: On upgrade/rollback—the marketplace requires zero-downtime upgrades if possible. How do you handle canary and rollbacks?
[05:58] Marcus: Our operator supports canary rollouts and traffic splitting at model and route level. For Private we enable A/B routing inside the operator by running two model replicas and doing traffic mirroring. Rollback is automatic on error thresholds or you can trigger manual rollback via the console or kubectl CRD.
[06:18] Priya: For air-gapped UAT, what's the recommended test plan?
[06:22] Avery: Recommended: 1) import OCI bundle to your registry, 2) run install in a staging namespace, 3) run a 7-day stability bench with representative traffic, 4) validate signed metering CSVs and SIEM forwarding, 5) exercise key rotation. We'll template the plan.
[06:38] Evan: About ingress/egress—do we need to open ports for model updates or is everything outbound TLS?
[06:44] Marcus: Everything is outbound TLS from the connector for model pulls in connected mode. But for operational snapshots (air-gapped) you import images. No inbound required.
[06:52] Lara: Any gotchas with service mesh? our mTLS and sidecars sometimes break init containers.
[06:58] Marcus: We recommend running the operator with sidecar injection disabled for operator pods and using a PodMutatingWebhook exception for our runtime pods. We have example manifests for Istio/Linkerd. We'll share those.
[07:12] Tom: Marketplace listing requires a short 'reference architecture' doc. can you provide a template that shows network diagrams and deployment steps?
[07:20] Avery: Yes we'll attach a tailored ref-arch doc showing both cloud-connected and fully air-gapped installs, plus a sample network diagram with ports and ACLs.
[07:30] Priya: One more question—do you support HSM backed KMS for encryption-at-rest keys for model weights cache?
[07:37] Marcus: Yes, we support envelope encryption where your HSM/KMS keeps the master key. Model shards in cache are encrypted with data keys derived from the master. We can integrate with PKCS#11 or use cloud HSM over private peering. We'll need to test latency for key unwrap since that affects cold starts.
[07:58] Evan: If we run the 7-day bench, what data do you need from our side?
[08:02] Marcus: We need representative traffic (RPS, sequences distribution), cluster size, GPU types, and firewall egress policies. If you can share a small trace file we'll replay it.
[08:14] Lara: Okay, let's talk timeline. We want a marketplace listing by end of Q4, and an internal air-gapped pilot before that. Is that feasible?
[08:23] Avery: Feasible if we start the on-prem POC next week. We can hit packaging checklist and a 7-day bench in ~3 weeks, then cut the listing artifacts. We'll target listing readiness by 2026-12-15.
[08:36] Tom: Competitors we've looked at—CloudWave had an auto-updater but their signing model was weak, LatencyWorks had better native sidecar integration but pricing was higher.
[08:47] Marcus: Noted. We think Redwood's hybrid packaging and KMS flexibility is a good middle ground.
[08:54] Lara: Alright let's recap next steps.
[08:58] Avery: Recap: Redwood shares checklist and operator chart (Avery), Marcus starts Private cluster bench and posts results (Marcus), Evan shares firewall rules and trace (Evan), Priya sends compliance Qs (Priya). We'll schedule follow-up for week of 2026-10-18.
[09:14] Tom: Great thanks everyone.
[09:16] Speaker 6: thanks bye.
[09:18] Avery: Thanks all.
